sentences.nl: Dat zijn werkwoorden die op scheidbare werkwoorden lijken, maar ze scheiden niet.
sentences.en: These are verbs that look like separable verbs, but they don't separate.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Dat zijn – Those are (lit. That are)  
• werkwoorden – verbs  
• die – that / which  
• op – on (used with *lijken* to mean "like/resemble")  
• scheidbare werkwoorden – separable verbs  
• lijken, – look / resemble,  
• maar – but  
• ze – they  
• scheiden – separate  
• niet. – not.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Subject-Verb Agreement with *Dat*:** In Dutch, the singular pronoun *dat* (that) is used with the plural verb *zijn* (are) to mean "those are" when introducing or identifying plural nouns (*Dat zijn werkwoorden*).  
• **Relative Clause Word Order:** The word *die* introduces a relative clause referring back to *werkwoorden*. In Dutch subordinate clauses, the conjugated verb (*lijken*) gets pushed to the very end of the clause.  
• **Fixed Preposition (*lijken op*):** The verb *lijken* (to seem/appear) combines with the preposition *op* to mean "to look like" or "to resemble."  
• **Extensions:**  
  – Dat zijn mensen die ik goed ken. (Those are people whom I know well.)  
  – Hij lijkt erg op zijn vader, maar hij is rustiger. (He looks a lot like his father, but he is calmer.)  
  – Dit zijn woorden die moeilijk te vertalen zijn. (These are words that are difficult to translate.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Dat zijn planten die op cactussen lijken, maar ze prikken niet. (Those are plants that look like cactuses, but they don't prick.)

sentences.nl: De vorige video was de laatste aflevering in Drenthe.
sentences.en: The previous video was the last episode in Drenthe.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **De** (The) **vorige** (previous) **video** (video) **was** (was) **de** (the) **laatste** (last) **aflevering** (episode) **in** (in) **Drenthe** (Drenthe).  
• *Natural translation: The previous video was the last episode in Drenthe.*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Adjective Inflection (-e ending):** Both *video* and *aflevering* are "de-words" (common gender). Because they are preceded by the definite article *de*, the adjectives *vorig* (previous) and *laatst* (last) must take an **-e** ending, becoming *vorige* and *laatste*.  
• **Simple Past Tense (Imperfectum):** *Was* is the singular past tense of the irregular verb *zijn* (to be).  
• **Extensions:**  
  – De **vorige** keer **was** erg gezellig. (The previous time was very cozy/fun.)  
  – Dit is de **laatste** trein naar Amsterdam. (This is the last train to Amsterdam.)  
  – Heb je de nieuwe **aflevering** al gezien? (Have you seen the new episode already?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• De vorige les was het laatste hoofdstuk van het boek. (The previous lesson was the last chapter of the book.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Drenthe** is a province in the northeast of the Netherlands. Unlike the bustling, densely populated *Randstad* (the western area including Amsterdam, Rotterdam, The Hague, and Utrecht), Drenthe is the most sparsely populated province. To the Dutch, it is famous for its quiet nature, cycling paths, heathlands, and prehistoric *hunebedden* (megalithic dolmens/tombs).

sentences.nl: Het was toen al laat, op de allerlaatste avond.
sentences.en: It was already late then, on the very last evening.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Het was** – It was  
• **toen** – then / at that time  
• **al** – already  
• **laat,** – late,  
• **op de** – on the  
• **allerlaatste** – very last  
• **avond.** – evening.  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **The prefix *aller-* for emphasis:** Adding *aller-* to a superlative (like *laatste* -> *allerlaatste*) means "the very..." or "the absolute...". Notice the *-e* at the end of *allerlaatste* because it precedes a *de*-word (*de avond*).  
• **Time markers (*toen* and *al*):** *Toen* refers to a specific moment in the past ("then" / "at that time"), while *al* means "already". In Dutch, time adverbs like these naturally cluster together in the middle of the sentence right after the conjugated verb (*was*).  
• **Preposition *op*:** Just like in English ("on that evening"), Dutch uses the preposition *op* when referring to a specific day or part of a day (*op de avond*, *op maandag*).  

**Extensions:**  
• Dit is mijn **allerbeste** vriend. (This is my very best friend.)  
• Hij woonde **toen al** in Amsterdam. (He already lived in Amsterdam at that time.)  
• We vertrekken **op de allereerste** dag van de vakantie. (We are leaving on the very first day of the vacation.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Het was toen al donker, op de allereerste ochtend van het jaar. (It was already dark then, on the very first morning of the year.)

sentences.nl: We zijn inmiddels een paar dagen verder en we zijn in Amsterdam.
sentences.en: It's now a few days later, and we're in Amsterdam.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **We** = We  
• **zijn** = are  
• **inmiddels** = meanwhile / by now  
• **een paar** = a few / a couple of  
• **dagen** = days  
• **verder** = further  
• **en** = and  
• **we zijn** = we are  
• **in Amsterdam** = in Amsterdam  
*(Natural translation: A few days have passed by now, and we are in Amsterdam.)*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **[Time period] + verder zijn:** Literally "to be [time] further." In English, we usually make "time" the subject ("A few days have passed"), whereas Dutch very commonly keeps the people as the subject ("We are a few days further [along in time]").  
• **Inmiddels:** This is a very common adverb meaning "in the meantime," "meanwhile," or "by now." It sits in the middle of the clause, right after the conjugated verb (*zijn*).  
• **Coordinating Conjunction (en):** The word *en* connects two main clauses without changing the normal Subject-Verb word order in the second clause (*...en we zijn...*).

**Extensions:**  
• We zijn **een jaar verder**. (A year has passed / We are a year further along.)  
• Ik ben **inmiddels** klaar met werken. (I am finished with work by now.)  
• **Een paar** weken geleden. (A few weeks ago.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• We zijn inmiddels twee uur verder en de trein is er nog steeds niet. (Two hours have passed by now and the train is still not here.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Using *"[tijd] verder zijn"* is a quintessential Dutch storytelling transition. You will hear it constantly in Dutch vlogs, reality TV, podcasts, and everyday updates (e.g., *"We zijn inmiddels een uurtje verder..."*). Mastering this phrase will immediately make your narrative Dutch sound much more natural and native-like.

sentences.nl: Martin staat op het station.
sentences.en: Martin is standing at the station.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Martin (Martin) staat (stands) op (on / at) het (the) station (station).  
• Natural English: "Martin is standing at the station" or simply "Martin is at the station."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Positional verbs for "to be":** Dutch frequently uses positional verbs like *staan* (to stand), *liggen* (to lie), and *zitten* (to sit) instead of the general verb *zijn* (to be) to describe where someone or something is located. Even if you would just say "Martin *is* at the station" in English, Dutch prefers *staat*.  
• **Preposition *op*:** For public spaces, hubs, or open areas like a train station, school, or work, Dutch uses the preposition *op* (literally "on") rather than *bij* or *in*.  
• **Extensions:**  
– Ik sta op de bushalte. (I am [standing] at the bus stop.)  
– Zij staat op het vliegveld. (She is [standing] at the airport.)  
– De trein staat op spoor vier. (The train is on track four.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Mijn zus staat al tien minuten op het perron. (My sister has been standing on the platform for ten minutes already.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, when someone says *het station* without specifying, they almost always mean the train station (operated mostly by the *NS* - Nederlandse Spoorwegen). Train travel is deeply integrated into daily Dutch life, and stations are major meeting points equipped with shops, supermarkets, and massive underground bicycle parking garages (*fietsenstallingen*).

sentences.nl: Hij wacht op Xing.
sentences.en: He's waiting for Xing.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Hij = He  
• wacht = waits / is waiting  
• op = on (here: for)  
• Xing = Xing  
• **Natural translation:** He is waiting for Xing.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Fixed Preposition (*wachten op*):** In English, you wait *for* someone, so it is tempting to use the Dutch word *voor*. However, the verb *wachten* (to wait) always takes the preposition **op** (literally "on").  
• **Verb Conjugation:** The infinitive is *wachten*. To get the stem, remove *-en* (*wacht*). Normally, the third-person singular (*hij/zij/het*) adds a *-t* to the stem, but since the stem already ends in a *-t*, you do not add a second one.  
• **Present Tense:** Dutch uses the simple present tense (*hij wacht*) for both "he waits" and the continuous "he is waiting."  
• **Extensions:**  
  – Ik wacht op de trein. (I am waiting for the train.)  
  – Wacht je op mij? (Are you waiting for me?)  
  – Wij wachten al een uur op het eten. (We have been waiting for the food for an hour already.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Zij wacht buiten op haar beste vriendin. (She is waiting outside for her best friend.)

Note: 'wachten op' is a verb with a fixed preposition, unlike inseparable verbs such as 'verwachten' (to expect) which take no preposition and no 'ge-' in the past participle.

sentences.nl: Zij komt deze week naar Amsterdam.
sentences.en: She's coming to Amsterdam this week.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Zij – She  
• komt – comes  
• deze week – this week  
• naar – to  
• Amsterdam – Amsterdam  
*(Natural translation: She is coming to Amsterdam this week.)*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Time before Place (TeMPo rule):** In Dutch, expressions of **T**ime (*deze week*) almost always come before expressions of **P**lace (*naar Amsterdam*). In English, you usually put the place first ("to Amsterdam this week"), so watch out for this reversed order in Dutch!  
• **Present Tense for Future:** Just like in English ("She is coming..."), Dutch very commonly uses the simple present tense (*komt*) combined with a future time marker (*deze week*) to talk about planned future events.  
• **Preposition *naar*:** When talking about movement toward a city, country, or general destination, Dutch uses *naar* (to).  
• **Demonstrative Pronoun *deze*:** The word for "this" is either *deze* or *dit*. Because *week* is a "de-word" (common gender: *de week*), it takes *deze*. 

**Extensions:**  
• Hij gaat morgen naar Rotterdam. (He is going to Rotterdam tomorrow.)  
• Wij komen deze maand naar Nederland. (We are coming to the Netherlands this month.)  
• Kom jij dit weekend naar het feest? (Are you coming to the party this weekend? — *Note: 'het feest' is a het-word, just like 'het weekend', so it uses 'dit' instead of 'deze'.*)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Mijn broer vliegt deze zomer naar Spanje. (My brother is flying to Spain this summer.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Pronoun Emphasis (*Zij* vs. *Ze*):** In everyday spoken and written Dutch, the unstressed pronoun *ze* is the default for "she." Using the full, stressed form *zij* adds deliberate emphasis, often to contrast her with someone else (e.g., *Hij blijft thuis, maar **zij** komt naar Amsterdam* – He is staying home, but **she** is coming to Amsterdam).

(Note on lesson topic: unlike inseparable verbs with prefixes like be-, ver-, or ont-, the simple verb 'komen' adds ge- in the past participle: 'gekomen', whereas an inseparable verb like 'bekomen' stays 'bekomen' without ge-).

sentences.nl: Het moet een romantisch weekje worden.
sentences.en: It's supposed to be a romantic week.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Het** (It) **moet** (must / has to) **een** (a) **romantisch** (romantic) **weekje** (little week) **worden** (become / be).  
• Natural translation: It is supposed to be a romantic week. / It’s going to be a romantic little week.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Diminutives (-je):** *Week* (week) is a *de*-word (*de week*), which becomes *het weekje* in the diminutive form. In Dutch, all diminutives are *het*-words. Adding *-je* to time periods makes the timeframe sound cozy, pleasant, or manageable.  
• **Adjective inflection:** Because *weekje* is a *het*-word and is preceded by the indefinite article *een*, the adjective *romantisch* does **not** take an *-e* ending (compare: *een romantische week* vs. *een romantisch weekje*).  
• **Modal verb + worden:** The modal verb *moet* (must/should) is in the second position, pushing the main verb *worden* (to become) to the very end of the sentence. Here, *moeten worden* expresses an intention, expectation, or plan ("is supposed to be").  
• **Extensions:**  
  – Het moet een gezellig avondje worden. (It is supposed to be a cozy little evening.)  
  – Het wordt een druk dagje morgen. (It is going to be a busy little day tomorrow.)  
  – Dat moet een groot feest worden. (That is supposed to become a big party.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• We hebben een hotel aan zee geboekt, want het moet een ontspannen weekendje worden. (We booked a hotel by the sea, because it is supposed to be a relaxing little weekend.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Dutch speakers frequently use diminutives for periods of time (*een dagje uit*, *een weekendje weg*, *een weekje vakantie*) not because the time is literally shorter, but to express anticipation, leisure, and *gezelligheid* (coziness). Calling a vacation *een weekje* makes it sound relaxing and informal.

sentences.nl: Ah, daar is ze.
sentences.en: Ah, there she is.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Ah – Ah  
• daar – there  
• is – is  
• ze – she  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Inversion (V2 Rule):** In Dutch, the conjugated verb generally stays in the second position. Because the sentence starts with the adverb of place *daar* (there) rather than the subject, the verb *is* comes next, and the subject *ze* (she) is pushed to the third position. Note that English actually does the exact same thing in this specific phrase ("There is she" -> "There she is", or with nouns: "There is the bus").  
• **Unstressed Pronoun:** *Ze* is the unstressed, everyday form of *zij* (she). You use *ze* in normal flow, and only use *zij* if you want to heavily emphasize that it is *her* and not someone else.  
• **Extensions:**  
– Hier ben ik. (Here I am.)  
– Daar zijn ze. (There they are.)  
– Ah, daar heb je hem. (Ah, there he is — *idiomatic*).  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Kijk, daar komt de trein eindelijk aan. (Look, there arrives the train finally / Look, the train is finally arriving.)

sentences.nl: Ze geven elkaar een kus.
sentences.en: They give each other a kiss.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Ze = They  
• geven = give  
• elkaar = each other  
• een kus = a kiss  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Reciprocal Pronoun (*elkaar*):** *Elkaar* means "each other" or "one another." It is used when two or more people perform the exact same action on one another. Here, it acts as the indirect object (to whom the kiss is given).  
• **Word Order:** This follows the standard Dutch main clause word order: Subject (*Ze*) + Verb (*geven*) + Indirect Object (*elkaar*) + Direct Object (*een kus*).  
• **Verb Phrase:** Instead of the single verb *kussen* (to kiss), Dutch very commonly uses the phrase *een kus geven* (to give a kiss).  

**Extensions:**  
• Wij helpen elkaar altijd. (We always help each other.)  
• Ze geven elkaar een knuffel. (They give each other a hug.)  
• Jullie kennen elkaar al lang. (You guys have known each other for a long time.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Aan het einde van het feest geven de vrienden elkaar een dikke knuffel. (At the end of the party, the friends give each other a big hug.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, it is traditional to greet friends and family (especially at birthdays or celebrations) by giving **three** kisses on the alternating cheeks (right, left, right). However, in casual everyday settings nowadays, one kiss or a quick hug is becoming much more common among younger generations.

sentences.nl: Wat leuk om eindelijk in Amsterdam te zijn, en wat spannend.
sentences.en: How nice to finally be in Amsterdam, and how exciting.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Wat leuk = How nice  
• om = to (in order to)  
• eindelijk = finally  
• in Amsterdam = in Amsterdam  
• te zijn = to be  
• en = and  
• wat spannend = how exciting  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Exclamations with "Wat"**: In Dutch, "Wat + adjective" is used to make exclamations equivalent to "How + adjective!" in English (e.g., *Wat leuk!* = How nice!, *Wat spannend!* = How exciting!).  
• **The "om ... te + infinitive" structure**: When you follow an adjective (like *leuk*) with a verb action (to be somewhere), you wrap the clause in *om ... te*. The *om* starts the clause, and *te* goes right before the infinitive verb at the very end (*om ... te zijn*).  
• **Extensions**:  
  – Wat fijn om je weer te zien! (How nice to see you again!)  
  – Het is moeilijk om Nederlands te leren. (It is difficult to learn Dutch.)  
  – Wat gek om hier eindelijk te staan. (How crazy to finally stand here.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Wat geweldig om eindelijk op vakantie te gaan, en wat rustgevend. (How wonderful to finally go on vacation, and how relaxing.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Leuk and Spannend**: *Leuk* is arguably the most common positive adjective in the Netherlands, used for everything from "nice" and "fun" to "cool." *Spannend* translates to "exciting," but it carries a nuance of suspense, anticipation, or "good nerves"—the Dutch use it very frequently when someone is starting a new job, taking a big trip, or waiting for important news.

sentences.nl: Een sollicitatiegesprek en een weekje met jou.
sentences.en: A job interview and a week with you.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Een** (A)  
• **sollicitatiegesprek** (job-application-conversation / job interview)  
• **en** (and)  
• **een** (a)  
• **weekje** (little week)  
• **met** (with)  
• **jou** (you).

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Compound Nouns:** *Sollicitatiegesprek* is a classic Dutch compound word made of *sollicitatie* (job application) + *gesprek* (conversation/talk).  
• **Affective Diminutive (*-je*):** Adding *-je* to *week* makes it *weekje* (little week). In Dutch, diminutives are often used for time periods not to make them physically smaller, but to make them sound cozy, casual, relaxing, or manageable.  
• **Stressed Pronoun (*jou*):** Because the pronoun follows a preposition (*met*), you must use the object pronoun. Here, the stressed form *jou* is used instead of the unstressed *je* to put special emphasis on the person ("with *you*").  

**Extensions:**  
• Ik heb morgen een belangrijk sollicitatiegesprek. (I have an important job interview tomorrow.)  
• We gaan een weekendje weg met zijn tweeën. (We are going away for a little weekend just the two of us.)  
• Ik wil dit moment graag met jou delen. (I would love to share this moment with you.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Na dat moeilijke sollicitatiegesprek ben ik echt toe aan een rustig dagje met jou. (After that difficult job interview, I am really ready for a quiet little day with you.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Using diminutives for time and leisure—like *een weekje weg* (a week away), *een dagje uit* (a day out), or *een uurtje slapen* (an hour of sleep)—is deeply ingrained in Dutch culture. It adds a sense of *gezelligheid* (coziness/pleasantness) and implies that the time spent will be relaxed and enjoyable.

sentences.nl: Ja, deze week wordt heel belangrijk voor Martin en Xing.
sentences.en: Yes, this week is going to be very important for Martin and Xing.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Ja** = Yes  
• **deze week** = this week  
• **wordt** = becomes (will be)  
• **heel belangrijk** = very important  
• **voor** = for  
• **Martin en Xing** = Martin and Xing  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Demonstrative Pronouns (*deze* vs. *dit*):** *Week* is a *de*-word (common gender), so it takes **deze** for "this." If it were a *het*-word (like *het jaar* - the year), you would use **dit** (*dit jaar* - this year).  
• **The verb *worden* for the future:** Literally, *worden* means "to become." However, in Dutch, the present tense of *worden* is very often used to express what something "is going to be" or "will be" in the future.  
• **Adverb *heel*:** When placed before an adjective (like *belangrijk*), *heel* means "very" and does not get an *-e* ending.  

**Extensions:**  
• Morgen wordt heel leuk voor de kinderen. (Tomorrow is going to be very fun for the kids.)  
• Dit jaar wordt heel druk voor mij. (This year will be very busy for me.)  
• Deze maand is erg belangrijk voor ons bedrijf. (This month is very important for our company.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ja, deze wedstrijd wordt heel spannend voor het hele team. (Yes, this match is going to be very exciting for the whole team.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• None.

sentences.nl: Het eerste weekje samen.
sentences.en: Their first week together.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Het – The (neuter)  
• eerste – first  
• weekje – little week  
• samen – together  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Diminutives change the article:** The base word *de week* (the week) is a common-gender noun. However, when you add the diminutive suffix *-je* to make *weekje* (little week), the word automatically becomes neuter and takes the article **het**.  
• **Adjective endings:** Even though *weekje* is a *het*-word, the adjective *eerste* (first) keeps its *-e* ending because it follows the definite article *het*. (Note: Ordinal numbers like *eerste* always end in *-e* anyway).  
• **Sentence fragment:** This is a noun phrase rather than a complete sentence with a verb, commonly used as a photo caption, title, or short dairy entry.  

• **Extra phrases:**  
– Het eerste jaar samen. (The first year together.)  
– Een leuk weekendje weg. (A nice little weekend away.)  
– Ons eerste huisje. (Our first little house.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ons eerste avondje samen in het nieuwe appartement was erg gezellig. (Our first cozy evening together in the new apartment was very nice.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The Dutch use diminutives (*-je, -tje, -pje*) constantly, not just to indicate physical smallness, but to make things sound cozy (*gezellig*), informal, or affectionate. Saying *het eerste weekje* instead of *de eerste week* makes the time spent together sound sweet, pleasant, and relaxed (often used for a new baby, a new puppy, or a couple's first vacation).

sentences.nl: En na deze week weten we of Xing in Nederland kan blijven of niet.
sentences.en: And after this week we'll know whether Xing can stay in the Netherlands or not.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• En = And  
• na deze week = after this week  
• weten we = know we  
• of = whether / if  
• Xing = Xing  
• in Nederland = in the Netherlands  
• kan blijven = can stay  
• of niet = or not

*(Natural English: "And after this week we'll know whether Xing can stay in the Netherlands or not.")*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Inversion (Verb-Subject):** The sentence starts with a time phrase (*na deze week*). Under the Dutch "V2 rule" (the conjugated verb must be the second element in the main clause), the verb *weten* comes before the subject *we*.  
• **Present Tense for Future:** Dutch very commonly uses the simple present tense (*weten we*) to talk about the future when a time marker (*na deze week*) makes the future context clear.  
• **Subordinate Clause with 'of':** Here, *of* means "whether/if". It introduces a subordinate clause, which pushes all the verbs in that clause (*kan blijven*) to the very end. 

**Extensions:**  
• *Morgen horen we of we het huis krijgen of niet.* (Tomorrow we will hear whether we get the house or not.)  
• *Na vandaag weet ik of ik moet werken.* (After today I will know if I have to work.)  
• *Zij vraagt of je vanavond kunt komen.* (She is asking whether you can come tonight.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Na dit gesprek horen we of hij bij het bedrijf mag blijven of niet. (After this meeting, we will hear whether he gets to stay at the company or not.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• *None.*

sentences.nl: Maar hoe ondergaat Xing de Nederlandse directheid?
sentences.en: But how will Xing take Dutch directness?
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Maar (But) | hoe (how) | ondergaat (undergoes / experiences) | Xing (Xing) | de Nederlandse (the Dutch) | directheid (directness)?  
• Natural translation: But how does Xing experience the Dutch directness?

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Question Word Order (Inversion):** When a question starts with a question word like *hoe* (how), the conjugated verb (*ondergaat*) comes immediately before the subject (*Xing*). Note that the conjunction *maar* (but) sits in "position zero" and does not affect the word order of the rest of the sentence.  
• **Verb Choice (*Ondergaan*):** The verb *ondergaan* is an inseparable prefix verb meaning "to undergo" or "to experience" (often implying something one passively endures or is subjected to). Note: There is a homonym *ondergaan* which is separable and means "to sink/go down" (like the sun), so context is key!  
• **Noun Suffix (*-heid*):** *Directheid* is formed by adding *-heid* to the adjective *direct*. This is the exact equivalent of the English suffix "-ness" and always creates a *de*-word (e.g., *de directheid*).  

**Extensions:**  
• Maar hoe ervaart hij het Nederlandse weer? (But how does he experience the Dutch weather?)  
• De patiënt ondergaat morgen een zware operatie. (The patient is undergoing a heavy operation tomorrow.)  
• Ik waardeer haar eerlijkheid en openheid. (I appreciate her honesty and openness.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Maar hoe ondergaat de nieuwe student de drukte in Amsterdam? (But how is the new student experiencing the hustle and bustle in Amsterdam?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Nederlandse directheid (Dutch directness):** The Dutch are globally famous for being extremely straightforward. They value *eerlijkheid* (honesty) and clarity over polite ambiguity. For expats and newcomers (like Xing in your sentence), this can initially feel blunt or rude, even though the Dutch view it as a sign of respect and transparency.

Because the stress is on the verb stem (-gaan) and not the prefix (onder-), the verb is inseparable: it does not split in the present tense, and its past participle does not get 'ge-'

sentences.nl: Kom je kamperen? vraagt Martin.
sentences.en: "Are you going camping?" Martin asks.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Kom (Come) je (you) kamperen? (to camp?) vraagt (asks) Martin (Martin).  
• Natural English: "Are you coming camping?" Martin asks.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Komen + Infinitive:** In Dutch, the verb *komen* (to come) can be combined directly with another verb in the infinitive form (without *te*) to indicate coming somewhere to do an activity.  
• **Question Inversion:** To form a yes/no question, the verb (*kom*) comes first, followed immediately by the subject (*je*). Notice that the second person singular drops the *-t* ending in inverted questions (it is *kom je*, not *komt je*).  
• **Reporting Clause Inversion:** When a quote comes before the speaker attribution, the reporting verb comes before the subject (*vraagt Martin* instead of *Martin vraagt*), because the quote itself counts as the first element of the sentence.  
• **Extensions:**  
  – Kom je vanavond eten? (Are you coming over to eat tonight?)  
  – Kom je morgen zwemmen? (Are you coming swimming tomorrow?)  
  – "Ga je mee?" vraagt Sarah. ("Are you coming along?" asks Sarah.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Kom je dit weekend bij ons logeren? vraagt oma. (Are you coming to stay with us this weekend? asks grandma.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• *Kamperen* is a massive part of Dutch holiday culture. The Netherlands has one of the highest densities of caravans and campervans in the world. In the summer, millions of Dutch people flock to campsites (*campings*) both domestically (like on the Wadden Islands or the Veluwe) and in southern Europe, especially France.

sentences.nl: Hoezo?
sentences.en: What do you mean?
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Hoezo = How-so (Hoe = how, zo = so / like that)  
• Natural meaning = "How come?" or "Why do you ask?"

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Compound Interrogative:** "Hoezo" is a fusion of the question word *hoe* (how) and the adverb *zo* (so).   
• **Usage vs. Waarom:** While *waarom* simply asks "why" (seeking a general reason), *hoezo* asks for the specific context, logic, or motive behind what the other person just said. It often implies slight surprise, confusion, or skepticism.  
• **Word Order:** It is most commonly used as a standalone one-word question, or placed at the beginning of a question followed by standard question inversion (Verb – Subject).  

**Extensions:**  
• Hoezo niet? (How come not? / Why not?)  
• Hoezo denk je dat? (What makes you think that? / Why do you think that?)  
• Hoezo moet ik dat doen? (How come I have to do that?)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Hoezo ga je vanavond niet mee naar het feestje? (How come you aren't coming along to the party tonight?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• *Hoezo?* is extremely common in everyday spoken Dutch and fits well with the culture of Dutch directness. However, watch your tone of voice: with a curious, upward inflection, it simply means "Why do you ask?". With a flat or sharp tone, it can sound defensive or confrontational, like "What is *that* supposed to mean?". Avoid using it as a standalone word in formal writing.

hoezo.meaning: how so? / what do you mean? / why?
hoezo.form_note: interrogative adverb made from 'hoe' (how) + 'zo' (so/like that); used on its own as a question to ask for clarification or express surprise

sentences.nl: Je hebt een tent bij je.
sentences.en: You've brought a tent.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Je** – You  
• **hebt** – have  
• **een** – a  
• **tent** – tent  
• **bij** – with / by  
• **je.** – you.  

*(Natural translation: You have a tent with you.)*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Idiom "iets bij zich hebben" (to have something on/with oneself):** In Dutch, to say you are carrying something with you, you use the verb *hebben* (to have) + the object + the preposition *bij* + an object pronoun that matches the subject (e.g., *Ik heb ... bij me*, *Je hebt ... bij je*, *Hij heeft ... bij zich*).  
• **Word Order:** This follows standard Dutch main clause word order: Subject (*Je*) + Verb (*hebt*) + Direct Object (*een tent*) + Prepositional Phrase (*bij je*).

**Extensions:**  
• Ik heb geen contant geld bij me. (I don't have any cash on me.)  
• Heb je je paspoort bij je? (Do you have your passport with you?)  
• Zij heeft altijd een paraplu bij zich. (She always has an umbrella with her.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Vergeet niet dat je een regenjas bij je hebt! (Don't forget that you have a raincoat with you!)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Camping Culture (*Kamperen*):** The Dutch are avid campers. Every summer, a huge portion of the population heads out with tents, caravans, or folding trailers (*vouwwagens*), often to France, Germany, or domestic campsites (*campings*). Note that wild camping (*wildkamperen*)—simply pitching the tent you have with you in nature—is strictly illegal in the Netherlands and carries a hefty fine. You must use designated campsites.

sentences.nl: Hij wijst naar haar jurk en hij moet hard lachen.
sentences.en: He points at her dress and can't help laughing out loud.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Hij** – He  
• **wijst** – points  
• **naar** – to / at  
• **haar jurk** – her dress  
• **en** – and  
• **hij** – he  
• **moet** – must / has to  
• **hard** – loudly / hard  
• **lachen** – laugh  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Preposition Combination:** The verb *wijzen* (to point) is almost always paired with the preposition *naar* when indicating the direction or object being pointed at (*wijzen naar* = to point at/to).  
• **Idiom (*moeten lachen*):** While *moeten* literally means "must" or "have to," combining it with emotional or physical reactions like *lachen* (laugh) or *huilen* (cry) means that the reaction is involuntary. In natural English, *hij moet lachen* translates best as "he can't help but laugh" or "it makes him laugh."  
• **Adverb Use:** *Hard* is used here as an adverb meaning "loudly" or "intensely" (literally "hard").  
• **Coordinating Conjunction:** *En* (and) connects two main clauses without changing the standard Subject-Verb word order in the second clause (*hij moet...*).  

**Extensions:**  
• Zij wijst naar het bord. (She points at the sign.)  
• Ik moet altijd lachen om zijn grappen. (I always have to laugh at his jokes.)  
• De muziek staat veel te hard. (The music is way too loud.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Zij kijkt naar zijn nieuwe hoed en ze moet een beetje lachen. (She looks at his new hat and she can't help but laugh a little.)

sentences.nl: Wat overkomt haar nu?
sentences.en: What is happening to her now?
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Wat = What  
• overkomt = overcomes / befalls / happens to  
• haar = her  
• nu = now  

• **Chunk-by-chunk:** What | happens to | her | now?  
• **Natural translation:** What is happening to her now?

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Impersonal Verb (*overkomen*):** The verb *overkomen* means "to happen to (someone)" or "to befall (someone)." In this sentence, *wat* (what) is the grammatical subject, and the person experiencing the event (*haar* - her) is the indirect object. Because *overkomen* has an inseparable prefix (*over-*), the stress is on *komt* (overKOMT), and it does not split up in the sentence.  
• **Question Word Order:** Because *wat* is acting as the subject of the sentence here, it comes first, followed immediately by the conjugated verb (*overkomt*), the object (*haar*), and the time adverb (*nu*).  

**Extensions:**  
• *Dat overkomt mij nou altijd.* (That always happens to me.)  
• *Wat is jou overkomen?* (What happened to you? - *Note: In the perfect tense, it uses the auxiliary verb 'zijn' instead of 'hebben'.*)  
• *Het kan de beste overkomen.* (It can happen to the best of us.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Wat overkomt ons als we te laat komen? (What will happen to us if we arrive too late?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In everyday Dutch, asking *"Wat overkomt haar/hem/jou nu?"* is often used idiomatically to express surprise at someone's sudden strange behavior, very similar to the English *"What has gotten into her now?"* or *"What possesses her?"* Conversely, as a statement (*"Het overkwam me gewoon"* - It just happened to me), the Dutch use this verb to emphasize that an event was completely out of their control, often used when explaining away a mistake or an accident.

wat.form_note: Acts as the subject of the sentence here, so the verb takes the 3rd person singular form (stem + t).

overkomt.form_note: 3rd person singular present tense of the inseparable verb 'overkomen'. Because the stress is on the verb root (o-ver-KO-men), the prefix 'over-' is never separated in the present tense (unlike the separable verb 'OVERkomen' = to come over).

haar.form_note: 3rd person singular feminine object pronoun; acts as the indirect object (the person to whom something happens).
haar.fast_speech: Often reduced to /ər/ or /dər/ in casual speech: 'Wat overkomt d'r nu?'

nu.fast_speech: In spoken Dutch, 'nu' is often replaced by 'nou' (/nʌu/) in questions to express surprise or concern.

sentences.nl: Xing heeft speciaal een nieuwe jurk gekocht.
sentences.en: Xing bought a new dress specially.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Xing = Xing  
• heeft = has  
• speciaal = especially / specifically  
• een = a  
• nieuwe = new  
• jurk = dress  
• gekocht = bought  

(Natural English: "Xing bought a new dress especially [for this/the occasion].")

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Present Perfect Tense (Voltooid Tegenwoordige Tijd):** Dutch uses this tense for most past actions. The auxiliary verb *heeft* (from *hebben*) sits in the second position, and the past participle *gekocht* (from the irregular verb *kopen*) goes to the very end of the sentence.  
• **Adjective Inflection:** *Jurk* is a common gender (*de*) noun. However, even with an indefinite article (*een*), *de*-words always take an *-e* at the end of the adjective (*nieuw* becomes *nieuwe*).  
• **Adverb Placement:** The adverb *speciaal* is placed directly after the conjugated verb (*heeft*) and before the direct object (*een nieuwe jurk*) to emphasize the intention behind the action.  

• *Ik heb gisteren een leuke jas gekocht.* (I bought a nice coat yesterday.)  
• *Hij heeft speciaal voor jou gekookt.* (He cooked especially for you.)  
• *Zij heeft een dure auto gekocht.* (She bought an expensive car.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Wij hebben speciaal voor het feest een grote taart gekocht. (We bought a big cake especially for the party.)

heeft.meaning: has (used with 'gekocht' to form the present perfect tense: 'bought')
heeft.form_note: 3rd person singular (hij/zij) present tense of the irregular verb 'hebben', acting as the auxiliary verb for the present perfect
heeft.fast_speech: in casual speech, the final -t may be dropped before a consonant: /ɦeːf/

speciaal.form_note: adverbial form (uninflected) modifying the action of buying

een.form_note: indefinite article used before singular countable nouns of both genders (de and het)
een.fast_speech: always unstressed in this meaning; the -n is often dropped before consonants: /ə/

nieuwe.form_note: inflected form of 'nieuw': takes an -e ending because it stands before a singular de-word ('de jurk')

jurk.form_note: singular common-gender noun (de-word), direct object of the sentence
jurk.fast_speech: an extra schwa is often heard between 'r' and 'k': /ˈjʏrək/

gekocht.form_note: irregular past participle of 'kopen'. Note the contrast with this lesson's grammar: 'kopen' is a normal base verb so its participle gets 'ge-', whereas an inseparable compound like 'verkopen' (to sell) has stress on the verb stem and takes NO 'ge-' (past participle: 'verkocht')

sentences.nl: Ze wil dat Martin haar mooi vindt.
sentences.en: She wants Martin to find her beautiful.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Ze – She  
• wil – wants  
• dat – that  
• Martin – Martin  
• haar – her  
• mooi – pretty / beautiful  
• vindt – finds  

(Natural English: She wants Martin to find her pretty / She wants Martin to think she is beautiful.)

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **"Wil dat..." Construction:** Unlike English, which uses an object + infinitive ("wants Martin to find"), Dutch requires a subordinate clause introduced by *dat* ("wants that Martin finds").  
• **Subordinate Clause Word Order:** The word *dat* pushes the conjugated verb of the second clause (*vindt*) all the way to the end of the sentence.  
• **The Verb *Vinden*:** While it literally means "to find", *vinden* is standardly used in Dutch to express an opinion, equivalent to "to think" or "to consider" in English.  
• **Irregular Verb *Willen*:** Note that the third-person singular of *willen* (to want) is *hij/ze wil*, without the standard *-t* ending.  

**Extensions:**  
• Ik wil dat je naar mij luistert. (I want you to listen to me.)  
• Hij denkt dat zij hem aardig vindt. (He thinks that she likes him / finds him nice.)  
• We willen dat het feest leuk wordt. (We want the party to be fun.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Hij wil dat zijn baas hem slim vindt. (He wants his boss to think he is smart.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, expressing opinions is very common and direct. Using the verb *vinden* (e.g., *Ik vind het mooi* - I think it's pretty) is the most natural and daily way to state personal taste or subjective thoughts without sounding like you are stating an absolute fact.

ze.form_note: unstressed 3rd person singular feminine subject pronoun (stressed form: zij); acts as the subject of the main clause

wil.form_note: 3rd person singular (zij/ze) present tense of the modal verb willen; irregular: no -t ending in the 3rd person singular

dat.meaning: that (introduces the subordinate clause; in English translated with 'Martin to find...')
dat.form_note: subordinating conjunction (onderschikkend voegwoord): sends the conjugated verb 'vindt' to the very end of the subordinate clause
dat.fast_speech: Before 'Martin', the final /t/ is often unreleased or assimilates to /p/: /dɑp ˈmɑrtɪn/

martin.form_note: singular proper noun; acts as the subject of the subordinate clause introduced by 'dat'

haar.form_note: 3rd person singular feminine object pronoun; acts as the direct object of 'vindt' in the subordinate clause
haar.fast_speech: In unstressed fast speech, often reduced to 'd'r' /dər/ or /ər/

mooi.form_note: uninflected base form (no -e ending) because it is used as an object complement (predicatively) with 'haar vindt' ('finds her beautiful')

vindt.meaning: finds (has the opinion that she is)
vindt.form_note: 3rd person singular (Martin = hij) present tense of the strong verb vinden: stem 'vind' + -t -> 'vindt' (pronounced /t/ at the end); placed at the end of the clause because of 'dat'. (Note for Lesson 32: compare 'vinden' -> 'gevonden' with inseparable verbs like 'bevinden' -> 'bevonden' which take no ge-)
vindt.fast_speech: The 'dt' spelling is pronounced simply as a single /t/: /vɪnt/

sentences.nl: Vind je mijn jurk niet mooi?
sentences.en: Don't you like my dress?
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Vind** – Find (think/consider)  
• **je** – you  
• **mijn** – my  
• **jurk** – dress  
• **niet** – not  
• **mooi?** – beautiful / pretty?  
*(Natural translation: Don't you like my dress? / Don't you think my dress is pretty?)*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Verb-first for questions (Inversion):** To make a yes/no question in Dutch, put the conjugated verb (*vind*) first, followed immediately by the subject (*je*).  
• **Dropping the '-t' with 'je':** Normally, the verb *vinden* gets a *-t* for the second person (*jij vindt*). However, when *je* or *jij* comes **after** the verb in a question, the *-t* is dropped (*Vind je...*).  
• **The "vinden + adjective" structure:** Dutch doesn't have a single verb for "to like" (for objects). Instead, you say you "find" something "nice/good/pretty."  
• **Placement of 'niet':** When negating an adjective (*mooi*), the word *niet* goes directly in front of that adjective.  

**Extensions:**  
• *Vind je de soep niet lekker?* (Don't you like the soup? / Don't you find the soup tasty?)  
• *Vind je deze film niet saai?* (Don't you think this movie is boring?)  
• *Ik vind jouw nieuwe schoenen erg mooi.* (I really like your new shoes / I find your new shoes very pretty.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Vind je dit schilderij niet een beetje vreemd? (Don't you find this painting a bit strange?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Dutch Directness:** While this question in English is often a "trap" fishing for a polite compliment, Dutch culture values honesty and directness. If you ask a Dutch person this question, be prepared for a literal, honest answer—such as *"Nee, de kleur staat je niet zo goed"* (No, the color doesn't suit you very well)—which is meant to be helpful rather than rude.

vind.meaning: find / think (used here to express an opinion: 'do you find/like')
vind.form_note: 2nd person singular (jij) present tense of 'vinden' with inversion: the -t is dropped because the subject 'je' comes right after the verb
vind.fast_speech: together with 'je', /t/ + /j/ often merges into a 'ch' sound: /ˈvɪntjə/ or /ˈvɪɲcə/

je.form_note: unstressed form of the subject pronoun 'jij', placed after the verb to form a question (inversion)

mijn.fast_speech: in casual speech almost always reduced to m'n: /mən/

jurk.form_note: singular common-gender noun (de-word), direct object of 'vind'
jurk.fast_speech: a tiny schwa sound is often heard between /r/ and /k/: /ˈjʏrək/

niet.form_note: negation adverb; placed directly before the adjective 'mooi' that it negates

mooi.form_note: predicative adjective (uninflected, no -e ending) describing the direct object 'mijn jurk' in the construction 'iets mooi vinden' (to like the look of something)

sentences.nl: Martin aanschouwt de jurk.
sentences.en: Martin looks the dress over.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Martin: Martin  
• aanschouwt: beholds / observes / gazes at  
• de: the  
• jurk: dress  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Verb Choice and Conjugation:** The verb used here is *aanschouwen* (to behold, to contemplate, to gaze upon). Because the prefix *aan-* is unstressed in this specific verb (aan**schou**wen), it is an inseparable verb. For the third-person singular (Martin), you take the stem (*aanschouw*) and add *-t* (*aanschouwt*).  
• **Transitivity:** Unlike the common verb for looking (*kijken naar* - to look at), *aanschouwen* is transitive and takes a direct object without a preposition.  
• **Noun Gender:** *Jurk* is a common gender noun, so it uses the definite article *de*.  
• **Extensions:**  
  – De toeristen aanschouwen het oude kasteel. (The tourists behold the old castle.)  
  – Zij draagt een prachtige rode jurk. (She is wearing a beautiful red dress.)  
  – Hij aanschouwt het kunstwerk in stilte. (He gazes at the artwork in silence.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• De koningin aanschouwt de nieuwe collectie. (The queen beholds the new collection.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The verb *aanschouwen* is very formal, poetic, or archaic in modern Dutch. In everyday conversation, a Dutch speaker would simply say *Martin bekijkt de jurk* (Martin examines/looks at the dress) or *Martin kijkt naar de jurk* (Martin looks at the dress). Using *aanschouwt* for something ordinary like a dress today usually implies irony, dramatic flair, or deep awe.

aanschouwt.form_note: 3rd person singular present tense of the inseparable verb 'aanschouwen' (stem 'aanschouw' + t). Even though 'aan-' is usually separable, here the stress is on the verb part (-schouw-), so it never splits and gets no 'ge-' in the past participle.

de.form_note: definite article for singular common gender (de-words) like 'jurk'

jurk.form_note: singular common gender noun (de-word), direct object of the sentence
jurk.fast_speech: often pronounced with a tiny schwa between r and k: /ˈjʏrək/

sentences.nl: Om eerlijk te zijn, ik vind die jurk verschrikkelijk, en dan overdrijf ik niet.
sentences.en: To be honest, I think that dress is awful, and I'm not exaggerating.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Om eerlijk te zijn,** = In order honest to be (To be honest,)  
• **ik vind** = I find  
• **die jurk** = that dress  
• **verschrikkelijk,** = terrible,  
• **en dan** = and then  
• **overdrijf ik niet.** = exaggerate I not (I am not exaggerating).

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **The *Om ... te* + Infinitive Construction:** Usually used to express purpose ("in order to"), here *Om eerlijk te zijn* acts as a fixed introductory phrase meaning "To be honest."  
• **Lack of Inversion (Spoken Style):** Normally, starting a sentence with an *om... te* clause triggers subject-verb inversion in the main clause (*Om eerlijk te zijn, **vind ik**...*). However, in casual spoken Dutch, people often pause after this specific phrase and use normal word order (**ik vind**), treating the intro as a separate thought.  
• **Inversion after *En dan*:** In the second part, *en* is a coordinating conjunction (which doesn't change word order), followed immediately by the adverb *dan* (then). Because the clause starts with *dan*, the verb (*overdrijf*) and subject (*ik*) must invert: *dan overdrijf ik*.  
• **Idiomatic clause:** *En dan overdrijf ik niet* (literally "and then I don't exaggerate") is the standard Dutch way to say "and I'm not exaggerating" or "and that's no exaggeration."

**Extensions:**  
• Om eerlijk te zijn, heb ik daar vandaag geen zin in. (To be honest, I don't feel like doing that today. — *Note the standard inversion here: heb ik*.)  
• Ik vind die film echt verschrikkelijk saai. (I find that movie really terribly boring.)  
• Het duurde uren, en dan overdrijf ik niet! (It took hours, and I'm not exaggerating!)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Om eerlijk te zijn, ik vind het eten hier vies, en dan overdrijf ik niet. (To be honest, I think the food here is gross, and I'm not exaggerating.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Dutch Directness (*Directheid*):** The Dutch are culturally known for valuing honesty and straightforwardness over polite sugarcoating. If a friend asks for an opinion on an outfit, a blunt response like this is much more acceptable in the Netherlands than in many Anglo-Saxon cultures. Using *vinden* (to find/think) softens it slightly by framing it clearly as a personal opinion rather than an absolute fact.

om.form_note: forms the infinitive construction 'om ... te + infinitive' (to be honest)

eerlijk.form_note: predicate adjective after 'zijn', so it takes no -e ending

te.form_note: infinitive marker used with 'om' before the infinitive verb 'zijn'

zijn.form_note: infinitive form of the irregular verb 'zijn', following 'te'

ik.form_note: 1st person singular subject pronoun, placed after the verb due to inversion after 'dan'

die.form_note: demonstrative determiner used before a singular de-word ('jurk')

verschrikkelijk.form_note: predicate adjective describing the object 'die jurk', so no -e ending
verschrikkelijk.fast_speech: first schwa is often dropped or very short: /fˈsxrɪkələk/

en.form_note: coordinating conjunction connecting the two main clauses

dan.form_note: adverb placed at the start of the clause, triggering inversion of the verb ('overdrijf') and subject ('ik')

overdrijf.form_note: 1st person singular (ik) present tense of the inseparable verb 'overdrijven' (stress is on the verb stem '-drijf', so the prefix 'over-' never splits off, and the past participle 'overdreven' takes no ge-)
overdrijf.fast_speech: followed by 'ik', final /f/ often voices slightly or links smoothly: /oːvərˈdrɛifɪk/

niet.form_note: negation adverb placed at the end of the clause to negate the verb 'overdrijf'

collocations.en: (in order) to … — the Dutch infinitive clause

sentences.nl: Dat overtreft alles.
sentences.en: That beats everything.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Dat (That) overtreft (surpasses / exceeds) alles (everything).  
• Natural English: "That beats everything." / "That takes the cake."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Word Order & Structure:** This is a simple Subject-Verb-Object (SVO) main clause.  
• **Verb Choice:** *Overtreffen* (to surpass, exceed, or outdo) is a strong verb with an inseparable prefix (*over-*). Because the prefix is inseparable, the stress falls on the root (*over**tref**fen*), and the past participle does not get a *ge-* prefix (past tense: *overtrof*, past participle: *overtroffen*).  
• **Pronoun Usage:** *Dat* (that) refers to a previously mentioned event or situation. Even though *alles* (everything) encompasses many things, it is grammatically singular in Dutch.  
• **Extensions:**  
  – Dit overtreft mijn stoutste verwachtingen. (This exceeds my wildest expectations.)  
  – Zij overtreft haar leraar in snelheid. (She surpasses her teacher in speed.)  
  – Dat slaat echt alles! (That really beats everything! — *a very common, slightly more informal synonym using the verb "slaan" [to hit]*).

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Het uitzicht vanaf de bergtop overtreft al onze dromen. (The view from the mountain top surpasses all our dreams.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• While *Dat overtreft alles* is often used positively to mean something is exceptionally good, the closely related idiom *Dat slaat alles* is almost exclusively used to express shock, disbelief, or annoyance at someone's ridiculous behavior (similar to "That takes the cake" in English). *Overtreffen* sounds slightly more formal or poetic than *slaan*.

dat.meaning: that (subject of the sentence, referring to a previously mentioned thing or situation)
dat.form_note: singular demonstrative pronoun; triggers third-person singular verb conjugation

overtreft.form_note: 3rd person singular present tense of the inseparable verb 'overtreffen' (stem 'overtref' + -t). Because the stress is on the verb part (-treffen) and not on the prefix (over-), this verb is inseparable: it does not split in the present tense ('dat overtreft', NOT 'dat treft over') and gets no 'ge-' in the past participle ('overtroffen').

alles.form_note: invariable singular indefinite pronoun referring to things as a whole

sentences.nl: Xing is helemaal beduusd.
sentences.en: Xing is completely stunned.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Xing = Xing  
• is = is  
• helemaal = completely / totally  
• beduusd = dazed / stunned / bewildered  
• **Natural translation:** Xing is completely stunned / bewildered.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Main clause word order:** This sentence follows the standard Subject-Verb-Object/Complement order: *Xing* (subject) + *is* (verb, from *zijn*) + *helemaal beduusd* (predicate adjective).  
• **Adjective without -e:** Because *beduusd* comes after a linking verb (*is*) and is not placed directly in front of a noun, it does not take the *-e* ending.  
• **Intensifier *helemaal*:** *Helemaal* acts as an adverb modifying the adjective *beduusd*. It is very common in spoken Dutch to emphasize a state of being (similar to "completely" or "totally").  

**Extensions:**  
• Ik ben helemaal kapot. (I am completely exhausted / broken.)  
• Zij was helemaal in de war. (She was completely confused.)  
• Na het ongeluk keek hij beduusd om zich heen. (After the accident, he looked around in a daze.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• De kat was helemaal beduusd na zijn val van de tafel. (The cat was completely stunned after his fall from the table.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Nuance of *beduusd*:** While you can use words like *verbaasd* (surprised) or *geschokt* (shocked), *beduusd* specifically captures that quiet, slightly groggy, or speechless state right after something unexpected happens—like waking up from a deep nap or hearing sudden, overwhelming news. It sounds slightly endearing and expressive in everyday conversation.

is.form_note: 3rd person singular (hij/zij) present tense of the irregular verb 'zijn' (to be), used here as a linking verb (or auxiliary of state)

helemaal.fast_speech: often pronounced with the stress shifted to the first syllable when emphasizing: /ˈɦeːləmaːl/

beduusd.form_note: adjective, used predicatively after 'is' (no -e). It looks like a participle (be- … -d), but Dutch uses it only as an adjective.
beduusd.fast_speech: final -d is devoiced and pronounced as /t/

sentences.nl: Dit is geen romantisch weerzien.
sentences.en: This is not a romantic reunion.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Dit (This) is (is) geen (no / not a) romantisch (romantic) weerzien (reunion / seeing-again).  
• Natural translation: "This is not a romantic reunion."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Negation with *geen*:** In Dutch, you use *geen* instead of *niet* to negate indefinite nouns (nouns that would have *een* in front of them, or plural/uncountable nouns with no article). Think of *geen* as meaning "not a" or "no".  
• **Adjective inflection (missing *-e*):** The noun *weerzien* (from the verb *weerzien*, meaning "to see again") is a *het*-word (neuter). When an adjective comes before an indefinite *het*-word (after *een*, *geen*, *elk*, etc.), it does **not** get an *-e* ending. Thus, it is *geen romantisch weerzien* instead of *romantische*.  
• **Extensions:**  
  – Dit is geen goed idee. (This is not a good idea.)  
  – Het was een gelukkig weerzien. (It was a happy reunion.)  
  – Dat is geen groot probleem. (That is not a big problem.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Na tien jaar was het een emotioneel weerzien op het vliegveld. (After ten years, it was an emotional reunion at the airport.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• *Weerzien* is closely related to the standard, slightly formal Dutch farewell *Tot ziens* ("Until [we] see [each other again]") and the more poetic/formal *Tot wederziens*. While *reünie* is used for organized events (like a high school reunion), *weerzien* focuses on the emotional act of seeing someone again after a long time apart.

dit.form_note: subject of the sentence; neuter singular demonstrative pronoun used to introduce or identify a noun

is.form_note: 3rd person singular present tense of 'zijn' (irregular verb), linking the subject 'dit' to the predicate

geen.form_note: indefinite negation; used instead of 'niet een' to negate the indefinite noun phrase 'romantisch weerzien'

romantisch.form_note: attributive adjective without -e ending because it modifies an indefinite neuter singular noun ('het weerzien') preceded by 'geen'

weerzien.form_note: singular neuter noun ('het weerzien') made directly from the infinitive of the verb 'weerzien'. Note on the lesson grammar: as an infinitive noun, the stress is on 'weer-'; in finite forms it splits ('wij zien elkaar weer'), though its participle 'weergezien' exists alongside inseparable patterns.

sentences.nl: Dit aanvaardt ze niet en ze wordt boos.
sentences.en: She won't accept this, and she gets angry.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Dit (This) | aanvaardt (accepts) | ze (she) | niet (not) | en (and) | ze (she) | wordt (becomes) | boos (angry).  
• Natural English: "She does not accept this, and she gets angry."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **V2 Word Order and Inversion:** In Dutch main clauses, the conjugated verb must always be in the second position (V2). Because the sentence begins with the direct object *Dit* (This) for emphasis, the subject *ze* (she) and the verb *aanvaardt* (accepts) must invert so the verb stays in the second spot (*Dit aanvaardt ze...* instead of *Ze aanvaardt dit...*).  
• **DT-rule in Present Tense:** The verb is *aanvaarden* (to accept). The stem ends in a *-d* (*aanvaard*). Because the subject is third-person singular (*ze*), you still add the standard *-t* ending, resulting in the *-dt* spelling (*aanvaardt*). The d and t are pronounced as a single "t" sound.  
• **Worden + Adjective:** The verb *worden* means "to become" or "to get" when paired with an adjective like *boos* (angry).  

**Extensions:**  
• Dat gelooft hij niet. (He does not believe that. — *Object-Verb-Subject inversion*)  
• Zij wordt altijd snel moe. (She always gets tired quickly. — *Using 'worden' + adjective*)  
• Dit begrijp ik helemaal niet. (I do not understand this at all. — *Object-Verb-Subject inversion*)

## 3. Create a New Example

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)

In everyday spoken Dutch in the Netherlands, people strongly prefer the verb *accepteren* ("Dit accepteert ze niet"). In Belgium (Flanders), however, *aanvaarden* is much more commonly used in daily speech.

sentences.nl: Martin, waarom doe je dat?
sentences.en: Martin, why are you doing that?

## 1. Literal Translation  
• Martin, = Martin,  
• waarom = why  
• doe = do  
• je = you  
• dat? = that?

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Inversion in Questions:** When a question starts with a question word (*waarom*), the verb (*doe*) must come next, followed immediately by the subject (*je*).  
• **Dropped "T" in Inversion:** Normally, the second-person singular (jij/je) form of *doen* (to do) is *jij doet*. However, in Dutch, when *je* or *jij* comes **after** the verb (inversion), the verb drops its *-t* ending. Thus, *je doet* becomes *doe je*.  
• **Present Tense for Continuous Action:** Dutch uses the simple present (*doe je*) where English uses the present continuous ("are you doing").  

• Waarom zeg je dat? (Why are you saying that?)  
• Hoe doe je dat? (How do you do that?)  
• Wat doe je vandaag? (What are you doing today?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Lisa, waarom lach je zo hard? (Lisa, why are you laughing so loudly?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Dutch Directness:** Asking someone bluntly "Why are you doing that?" is very common in the Netherlands. While it might sound confrontational or critical in English-speaking cultures, the Dutch often ask it out of genuine curiosity or a desire for efficiency, without intending to be rude.

sentences.nl: Martin snapt niet wat hij verkeerd doet.
sentences.en: Martin doesn't get what he's doing wrong.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Martin (Martin) snapt (gets/understands) niet (not) wat (what) hij (he) verkeerd (wrongly/wrong) doet (does).  
• Natural translation: "Martin doesn't understand what he is doing wrong."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Subordinate Clause Word Order:** The second half of the sentence begins with the question word *wat* (what), which introduces an indirect question (a subordinate clause). In Dutch subordinate clauses, the conjugated verb is pushed to the very end of the clause (*wat hij verkeerd **doet***).  
• **Snappen vs. Begrijpen:** Both verbs mean "to understand," but *snappen* is more informal and conversational, very similar to saying "to get it" in English.  
• **Adverb Placement:** *Verkeerd* (wrongly) acts as an adverb modifying the verb *doet*, and in a subordinate clause, it sits directly before the final verb.

**Extensions:**  
• Ik snap niet wat je bedoelt. (I don't get what you mean.)  
• Zij weet niet wat ze verkeerd zegt. (She doesn't know what she is saying wrong.)  
• Snap jij waarom hij boos is? (Do you understand why he is angry?)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• De nieuwe student snapt nog niet hoe het systeem werkt. (The new student doesn't understand how the system works yet.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In daily Dutch conversation, you will hear *Ik snap het* (I get it) or *Snap je?* (Do you get it?) constantly. While *begrijpen* is taught first in many textbooks, using *snappen* will immediately make your spoken Dutch sound much more natural and native-like in casual settings.

sentences.nl: Ik omschrijf toch gewoon je jurk: een lelijke tent.
sentences.en: I'm just describing your dress: an ugly tent.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Ik (I) omschrijf (describe) toch (after all / right?) gewoon (simply / just) je (your) jurk (dress): een (an) lelijke (ugly) tent (tent).  
• Natural translation: I'm just describing your dress, aren't I: an ugly tent.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Modal Particles (*toch gewoon*):** The combination of *toch* and *gewoon* is very common in spoken Dutch. *Gewoon* means "simply" or "just", while *toch* seeks confirmation or expresses a defensive "after all." Together, they make the speaker sound like they are stating an obvious, innocent fact ("I'm just... right?").  
• **Inseparable verb (*omschrijven*):** *Omschrijven* (to describe) has an **inseparable** prefix here because the stress is on *schrij-* (om-SCHRIJ-ven). Therefore, in the present tense, the prefix *om* stays attached to the verb: *ik omschrijf*.  
• **Adjective Declension (*lelijke*):** *Tent* is a *de*-word (*de tent*). Even when using the indefinite article *een*, an adjective before a singular *de*-word gets an **-e** ending (*een lelijke tent*).

• **Extensions:**  
  – Ik zeg toch gewoon de waarheid? (I'm just telling the truth, right?)  
  – Kun je het probleem kort omschrijven? (Can you briefly describe the problem?)  
  – Hij kocht een lelijke jas. (He bought an ugly coat.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ik geef toch gewoon mijn mening: een saai boek. (I'm just giving my opinion, aren't I: a boring book.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Dutch Directness:** The Dutch are famous for being direct, and they often use the word *gewoon* (just/simply) to justify bluntness as mere honesty. However, calling someone's outfit "an ugly tent" crosses the line from typical Dutch directness into plain rudeness, likely meant here as harsh teasing among close friends or siblings.

sentences.nl: Maar wees niet boos.
sentences.en: But don't be angry.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Maar = But  
• wees = be (imperative)  
• niet = not  
• boos = angry / mad  
• Full translation: But don't be angry.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Irregular Imperative:** *Wees* is the irregular imperative (command) form of the verb *zijn* (to be). For most Dutch verbs, the imperative is simply the verb stem, but *zijn* is a special exception you must memorize.  
• **Word Order after "Maar":** Coordinating conjunctions like *maar* (but), *en* (and), and *want* (because) do not change the word order of the clause that follows. Therefore, the sentence keeps standard command structure: Verb (*wees*) + Negation (*niet*) + Adjective (*boos*).  
• **Extensions:**  
  – Wees voorzichtig! (Be careful!)  
  – Wees niet bang. (Don't be afraid.)  
  – Het is laat, maar maak je geen zorgen. (It is late, but don't worry.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ik heb een fout gemaakt, maar wees alsjeblieft niet teleurgesteld. (I made a mistake, but please don't be disappointed.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Using the imperative in Dutch (*wees...*) is very common and is not considered as blunt or rude as it sometimes can be in English. However, to soften the command in everyday conversation, Dutch speakers often insert the particle *even* or *alsjeblieft* (e.g., *Maar wees alsjeblieft niet boos*).

sentences.nl: Ik ben erg blij dat jij hier bent.
sentences.en: I'm really glad you're here.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Ik (I) ben (am) erg (very) blij (happy/glad) dat (that) jij (you) hier (here) *bent* (are).  
• Natural translation: I am very happy that you are here.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Subordinate Clause with *dat*:** The word *dat* (that) introduces a subordinate clause. In Dutch, the conjugated verb in a subordinate clause must be kicked to the very end of the clause. That is why *bent* (are) comes after *hier* (here), resulting in "...that you here are."  
• **Emphasis with *jij*:** Using *jij* instead of the unstressed *je* puts extra emphasis on the person ("I am glad that *you* are here").  
• **Intensifier *erg*:** Literally meaning "bad" or "severe," *erg* is very commonly used as an adverb meaning "very" (similar to *heel*).  

**Extensions:**  
• Ik ben blij dat het weekend is. (I am glad that it is the weekend.)  
• Zij is erg blij dat wij komen. (She is very happy that we are coming.)  
• We zijn blij dat je veilig thuis bent. (We are glad that you are home safely.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ik ben erg blij dat jij mij vandaag kunt helpen. (I am very glad that you can help me today.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Dutch people generally avoid over-the-top emotional expressions in everyday life, unlike the American tendency to use "amazing" or "thrilled." Saying *Ik ben erg blij dat...* is a genuinely warm, sincere, and very standard way to show appreciation when someone visits you or helps you out.

sentences.nl: Nederlanders zijn gewoon direct, en Amsterdammers helemaal.
sentences.en: Dutch people are just direct, and people from Amsterdam even more so.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Nederlanders (Dutch people) – zijn (are) – gewoon (simply/just) – direct, (direct,) – en (and) – Amsterdammers (people from Amsterdam) – helemaal (completely/especially so).

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Gewoon as a modal particle**: While *gewoon* literally means "normal" or "ordinary", here it is used as an adverbial filler word meaning "just" or "simply", softening the statement slightly while presenting it as a basic fact.  
• **Ellipsis with *helemaal***: The second clause (*en Amsterdammers helemaal*) drops the verb and adjective (*zijn direct*) to avoid repetition. *Helemaal* literally means "completely/totally", but in this trailing position, it translates best to "especially so", "even more so", or "all the more".  
• **Zero article with plural nationalities/demonyms**: Just like in English, plural nouns for groups of people (*Nederlanders*, *Amsterdammers*) do not require an article when making a general statement.  

**Extensions:**  
• De winter is koud, en januari helemaal. (Winter is cold, and January especially so.)  
• Hij is gewoon een beetje moe. (He is just a little tired.)  
• Belgen zijn vaak beleefd, en oudere mensen helemaal. (Belgians are often polite, and older people even more so.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Maandag is gewoon een drukke dag, en de ochtend helemaal. (Monday is simply a busy day, and the morning especially so.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• *Hollandse directheid* (Dutch directness) is a well-known cultural trait; the Dutch value honesty and straightforwardness over politeness, which foreigners sometimes mistake for rudeness. Within the Netherlands, people from Amsterdam (*Amsterdammers*) are stereotyped as being the most outspoken, blunt, and unapologetic of all, often delivering their directness with a dose of dry street humor.

sentences.nl: Wij zeggen wat we denken.
sentences.en: We say what we think.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Wij** (We - stressed) **zeggen** (say) **wat** (what) **we** (we - unstressed) **denken** (think).

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Wij vs. We:** Dutch has stressed (*wij*) and unstressed (*we*) subject pronouns. Starting a sentence with *Wij* emphasizes *who* is doing the action ("*We* [as opposed to others] say..."), while the second clause naturally shifts to the unstressed *we* because the emphasis is no longer needed.
• **Relative Pronoun "Wat":** Here, *wat* means "that which" or "the things that." Because it introduces a subordinate clause (*wat we denken*), the verb in that clause (*denken*) gets pushed to the very end. In this short clause, it just happens to follow the subject directly, but if you added an object or time, the verb would still go last.
• **Extensions:**  
  – *Zij doen wat ze willen.* (They do what they want.)  
  – *Ik eet wat ik lekker vind.* (I eat what I find delicious / what I like.)  
  – *Jullie horen wat jullie willen horen.* (You guys hear what you want to hear.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• *Hij koopt altijd wat hij nodig heeft.* (He always buys what he needs.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• This sentence perfectly sums up the famous *Nederlandse directheid* (Dutch directness). In the Netherlands, speaking your mind plainly is generally valued as honesty and transparency, rather than being seen as rude. A common related Dutch idiom is *"het hart op de tong hebben"* (to have the heart on the tongue), which means to always say what you are thinking.

sentences.nl: Nou, je overtuigt me niet helemaal.
sentences.en: Well, you don't quite convince me.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Nou, – Well,  
• je – you  
• overtuigt – convince  
• me – me  
• niet – not  
• helemaal. – completely / entirely.  
*(Natural translation: "Well, you haven't completely convinced me.")*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Soft Negation ("niet helemaal"):** Putting *niet* (not) before an adverb like *helemaal* (completely) creates a partial negation ("not completely/not quite"). This softens the statement, making it less harsh than a flat *niet* at the end of the sentence.  
• **Inseparable Verb:** The verb *overtuigen* (to convince) begins with the prefix *over-*. Here, the stress is on the verb stem (*over**tui**gen*), which means it is inseparable. In the present tense, it stays in one piece (*je overtuigt*), unlike separable verbs which split up.  
• **Discourse Marker ("Nou"):** *Nou* literally means "now," but at the start of a sentence, it functions like the English "Well..." to show hesitation, reflection, or slight doubt.

**Extensions:**  
• Ik begrijp het niet helemaal. (I don't completely understand it.)  
• Dat klopt niet helemaal. (That is not entirely correct.)  
• Hij overtuigt de jury met zijn verhaal. (He convinces the jury with his story.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Nou, dit plan werkt nog niet helemaal zoals ik wil. (Well, this plan isn't working quite the way I want yet.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• While the Dutch are famous for their directness, they heavily rely on "filler" words like *nou* (well), *eigenlijk* (actually), and *niet helemaal* (not entirely) in daily conversation to take the sharp edge off their honesty. Saying *"Nou, je overtuigt me niet helemaal"* is a very typical, polite-yet-direct Dutch way of saying "I think you're wrong" or "I don't buy it" during a meeting or discussion.

sentences.nl: Een vreemd gevoel overheerst bij Xing.
sentences.en: A strange feeling takes over in Xing.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Een** (A) **vreemd** (strange) **gevoel** (feeling) **overheerst** (dominates / prevails) **bij** (at / with) **Xing** (Xing).  
• *Natural translation:* A strange feeling prevails in Xing. / Xing is overcome by a strange feeling.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Adjective Ending (No *-e*):** *Gevoel* is a neuter noun (*het gevoel*). Because it is preceded by the indefinite article *een*, the adjective *vreemd* does not take an *-e* ending (so it is *een vreemd gevoel*, not *een vreemde gevoel*).  
• **The Verb *Overheersen*:** This is an inseparable prefix verb (*over-* + *heersen*), meaning to dominate, predominate, or prevail. Because the prefix is unstressed, the prefix stays attached in all tenses, and the past participle does not get *ge-* (*het heeft overheerst*).  
• **Preposition *Bij*:** When describing where an emotion, mood, or realization is taking place regarding a person or group, Dutch uses the preposition *bij* (literally "at/by/with").  

**Extensions:**  
• Teleurstelling overheerst bij het team na de wedstrijd. (Disappointment prevails among the team after the match.)  
• Ik heb een heel vreemd gevoel over deze situatie. (I have a very strange feeling about this situation.)  
• Blijdschap overheerst bij de winnaars. (Joy dominates among the winners.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Een diep gevoel van opluchting overheerst bij de studenten na het laatste examen. (A deep sense of relief prevails among the students after the final exam.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The phrasing *"[Emotie] overheerst bij [persoon/groep]"* is a hallmark of Dutch journalism, especially in sports reporting and political news. Reporters frequently use it right after a big event to summarize the collective mood (e.g., *"Trots overheerst bij Oranje"* – Pride prevails within the Dutch national team). Using it in casual conversation can sound slightly dramatic or literary.

sentences.nl: Dat zeg je toch niet als je blij bent elkaar weer te zien?
sentences.en: Surely you don't say that when you're happy to see each other again?
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Dat (That) zeg (say) je (you) toch (surely/after all) niet (not) als (when/if) je (you) blij (happy) bent (are) elkaar (each other) weer (again) te (to) zien (see)?

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Topicalization & Inversion:** The sentence starts with the object *Dat* for emphasis, which forces the verb (*zeg*) and the subject (*je*) to swap places (*zeg je* instead of *je zegt*). Note that in the *je*-inversion, the verb drops its *-t* ending.
• **Modal Particle *toch*:** Combined with *niet* and a question mark, *toch niet* acts like an English tag question ("You don't say that..., do you?"), seeking confirmation or expressing mild disbelief.
• **Subordinate Clause (*als*):** The conjunction *als* (when/if) pushes the conjugated verb (*bent*) toward the end of the clause (*als je blij bent*).
• **Adjective + *te* + Infinitive:** After adjectives of emotion like *blij*, Dutch connects the next action using *(om) ... te + infinitive*. Here, *om* is omitted: *[om] elkaar weer te zien*.

• **Extensions:**  
– Dat doe je toch niet op je werk? (You don't do that at work, do you?)  
– Ik ben zo blij je weer te horen. (I am so happy to hear from you again.)  
– Wat zeg je als je elkaar op straat tegenkomt? (What do you say when you run into each other on the street?)  

## 3. Create a New Example

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Dutch relies heavily on "modal particles"—short words like *toch*, *even*, *maar*, and *hoor* that don't have a single literal translation in English. They are the secret to sounding natural in Dutch because they soften the famous Dutch directness or add emotional nuance. Here, *toch* turns a blunt statement into a rhetorical, slightly scolding question.
